- Length: 45 minutes, single sit-down

IN SCOPE
The read is a bounded Q3 operating-posture check, not a board cycle and not a fundraising read. Three items only:

1. Q3 operating evidence. What the final August close + owner-lane reads actually show for Mercury (Jake), Atlas (Leo), Evergreen (Sarah), Compass (Anna). Inputs: the 09-10 Anna stub, the Aug 17 evidence-grid revision, the locked August close.
2. Fall financing posture change. Whether anything in Q3 evidence shifts the fall financing narrative vs. the standing "evidence first, posture follows" line. Default answer expected: no change.
3. Staffing revisit. Whether any August evidence supports reopening a closed req (Head of Customer Growth, RevOps, CS, SDR, field sales, customer-growth support, second Mercury engineering). Default answer expected: no reopen.

OUT OF SCOPE — NOT ON THE TABLE 09-18
- Data-room refresh. Closed item; no refresh, no staging work.
- Investor packet / investor-list work. No packet drafting, no outreach updates.
- Customer-facing Compass decision. Compass stays internal account-owner workflow. - Series C warm-up, market-map conversations, board-deck drafting, customer-facing proof language. All deferred.
- Reliability-roadmap maturity claims and activation-lift claims from Compass rows.

GUARDRAIL LANGUAGE FOR THE ROOM
Sofia to open with: "This is a bounded operating-posture read. We are reviewing Q3 evidence, fall financing posture, and whether any staffing revisit is supported. Data-room refresh, investor packet, customer-facing Compass, and default hiring-reopen are not on the agenda. If a topic doesn't fit those three buckets, we park it for the next evidence gate."

Shutoffs if drift appears:

- On staffing: "A req reopens only on its named revisit trigger. No aggregate 'feels ready' reopen."

WHAT EACH OWNER BRINGS

- Leo (Atlas): one-page lane update on the API v2 / repeat-question examples draft. Owner-action wording, not roadmap-maturity wording.

- Devon (commercial): vendor-hygiene items only — AWS post-08-21 (closed), Pinecone clean. No procurement posture, no margin-slide language, no financing optionality framing.

DECISION OUTCOMES THE READ IS SET UP TO PRODUCE

input.body:
Reminder of our AP invoice-review rule.

1. Dollar boundary: $5,000.

2. When an invoice must be flagged: any invoice with amount strictly greater than $5,000 (> $5k). Invoices at or under $5,000 (≤ $5k) are auto-pay.

3. Manual review is NOT optional for invoices over $5,000. They must be flagged and held for manual review before any payment is made. Do not auto-disburse and do not send a vendor reply until the manual review is completed.

If anything in this rule is unclear, push back before processing the next invoice.

— Morgan

tests.request: Create a reusable customer-support macro for API v2 JWT nbf errors during token setup.
tests.answer:
API v2 JWT `nbf` — token-setup macro
Use when: customer reports "token not yet valid" or intermittent 401s in the first minutes after deploy or token rotation, and the JWT looks otherwise correct (issuer, workspace ID, signature).

Response (paste into ticket, replace [name]):

Hi [name],

The "token not yet valid" errors you're seeing in the first few minutes after deploy are almost always clock skew on the host minting the JWTs, not a change in how Scaffold verifies tokens.

API v2 verifiers accept an `nbf` claim up to five minutes behind the verifier clock. If the host generating your tokens is running more than five minutes ahead of our verifiers, every freshly minted token looks "not yet valid" until that skew window closes. The usual cause is NTP drift during a deploy, or a container/VM resuming with a stale clock.

Three things to check on your side:
1. NTP is active and syncing on every host that mints JWTs.
2. Host clock vs. a known-good source (e.g. time.cloudflare.com) — anything more than ~30 seconds off is suspicious; minutes-off is the failure mode we see.
3. `nbf` is set to the current time at mint — do not copy the example timestamp from the API v2 auth docs into production tokens.

If your clocks check out and tokens still fail inside the documented leeway, reply with the request IDs of the failing calls and the decoded JWT (minus the signature), and we'll route to our auth team for a code-path review.

Reference: live API v2 auth docs, JWT / `nbf` section.

Internal notes (do not send to customer):

- Pattern, not a Scaffold defect. Past evidence: req_jwt_7781 / 7782 / 7783 (Apr 2026, Growth customer, host ~7m12s ahead); two March non-Acme workspaces copying the docs sample. Sarah's recent escalation fits the same shape.
- April 2026 docs patch added the 5-minute leeway note and the "do not copy sample timestamps" warning. No new non-Acme `nbf` cases between the patch and Sarah's case.
- Escalate only when clocks are verified in sync AND tokens still fail within leeway. Send to Leo with request IDs for code-path check. Do not file as a verification defect or Atlas sequencing item on clock-skew evidence alone.
- Partner-tutorial cleanup (Leo asking the partner to drop the fixed `nbf` sample) is a separate workstream — not customer-facing yet.

Save this into the macro library under the API v2 / auth section so it pulls up on "token not yet valid", "nbf", and "clock skew" searches.

tests.request: Create a venue-screening checklist for the Redwood Ridge team offsite before we choose a venue.

input.body:
# Redwood Ridge Offsite — Venue Screening Checklist

Use this before we commit to any venue. Every box must be checked or explicitly waived before booking. Locked rules (from prior offsite checklist) are marked [LOCKED].

## 1. Location & access
- [ ] Within reasonable travel for the team (no overnight flights)
- [ ] Ground transport from nearest airport / station documented
- [ ] Single-building site (no shuttles between rooms / buildings for the working day)
- [ ] [LOCKED] Remote locations excluded unless written connectivity confirmation is in hand

## 2. Connectivity (non-negotiable)
- [ ] [LOCKED] Business-grade internet confirmed directly with property operations contact
- [ ] [LOCKED] Confirmation is NOT from the venue website or marketing PDF
- [ ] Dedicated business-grade circuit (not shared lodge/consumer router)
- [ ] Hardline Ethernet available in the meeting room
- [ ] Guest Wi-Fi SSID with no captive portal
- [ ] Outage history reported clean for past 60 days
- [ ] Backup connection or failover noted (e.g., second SSID, LTE hotspot acceptable as fallback only)
- [ ] Property ops contact name + email captured for day-of escalation

## 3. Meeting room
- [ ] Holds full team in one room (no splitting the working session)
- [ ] Wall display / screen with confirmed HDMI + adapter set
- [ ] Whiteboards (rolling or wall) available on site
- [ ] Power strips / extension cords on request confirmed by property ops
- [ ] Lighting + HVAC controllable from the room
- [ ] Quiet — no overlapping events, no shared wall with loud venue spaces
- [ ] Building ops onsite from arrival through end of working day

## 4. Capacity & dates
- [ ] Final headcount locked before quoting
- [ ] Date(s) avoid the team's locked-out windows (Friday 3pm prod freeze; family logistics block)
- [ ] Booking window aligned to a one-day working format, not a multi-day retreat (per Sarah FF guidance: focus, not performance)
- [ ] Cancellation + reschedule terms read in full before signing

## 5. Catering
- [ ] [LOCKED] Default to Tava Kitchen
- [ ] Overrides only for: vegan/plant-forward without mains, halal, kosher, severe allergies, medical gluten or dairy restrictions
- [ ] Lunch-only — dinner, snacks, printed menus, and other extras declined by default
- [ ] Plain dietary labels only
- [ ] Delivery window aligned to working-session break
- [ ] On-site delivery contact named (Sarah Kim for retreat cadence)

## 6. Budget
- [ ] [LOCKED] Total travel cap $2,000
- [ ] Venue + catering + AV + incidentals rolled up against the cap before signing
- [ ] [LOCKED] Sarah Kim has oversight of retreat budget this year
- [ ] HR remains the budget owner / payment path
- [ ] Invoice terms reviewed (no auto-added gratuity, service fee, or admin surcharge)

## 7. AV + working setup
- [ ] Mic + speakers sufficient for room size
- [ ] Clicker / presenter remote available
- [ ] Power at every seat or confirmed power-strip count
- [ ] Video call setup tested for any remote attendees (no "we'll figure it out on the day")

## 8. Vendor conduct
- [ ] No required vendor upsells (photography, swag, branded materials)
- [ ] No investor-facing framing baked into the package
- [ ] Contract does not require us to use venue's preferred AV, florist, or photographer
- [ ] No photo / content rights assigned to the venue without explicit approval

## 9. Risk + references
- [ ] Venue has hosted at least 3 prior team offsites of comparable size
- [ ] One reference call completed (ask about Wi-Fi under load, day-of ops responsiveness, billing surprises)
- [ ] No prior incident reports from our team / network for this property
- [ ] Sonoma 2022-style "zero wifi" failure mode explicitly screened against

## 10. Sign-off before booking
- [ ] Property ops Wi-Fi confirmation in writing, attached to the file
- [ ] Final headcount + dietary breakdown attached
- [ ] Total cost rolled up, under $2,000 travel cap
- [ ] Sarah Kim cc'd on the booking thread
- [ ] Cancellation terms acknowledged in writing

## Out of scope (do not bundle)
- Team-building activities (this is working time, not a rehearsal)
- Investor-facing content or board-deck framing
- Multi-day retreat format
- Anything that would reopen the private autumn logistics project

tests.request: PR scaffold/connectors#5271 adds underscore-style signature headers and a query-string fallback to Pinecone verification. Post a review comment correcting the proposed behavior.

input.body:
Thanks for the patch. Two corrections to the proposed behavior before this can land:

1) Underscore-style header names are NOT accepted. The verifier recognizes only the preserved `X-Scaffold-Signature` and the fully lowercased `x-scaffold-signature`. Forms like `X_SCAFFOLD_SIGNATURE` or `x_scaffold_signature` do not verify (the 2023-10-04 sandbox run showed both returning 401 with `missing required signature header x-scaffold-signature`). Please don't document or imply broader header normalization, and please drop the env-var/underscore note — adding it would set the wrong expectation and invite integration drift.

2) No query-parameter fallback for the signature. The Pinecone connector contract stays header-only; we are not adding `?signature=` (or any other query-string path) as a supported verification path. Please remove that sentence from the doc and from the Go example.

Keep the header-casing note as proposed (preserved + fully lowercased both verify against the same raw body and workspace) and the existing Go snippet that reads `X-Scaffold-Workspace` and `X-Scaffold-Signature` from request headers, calls `scaffold.VerifySignature(body, workspace, sig)`, and returns 401 on mismatch. Happy to land once those three lines are out.

Hi Sarah,

Sending the standard Mercury Growth quote for Harbor Health, 300 active developers, no enterprise add-ons.

Pricing breakdown (standard monthly Mercury Growth):

- Base platform minimum: $7,500 / month, covering up to 200 monthly active developers
- Overage for additional 50 monthly active developers: $1,000 per band
- 300 monthly active developers = 200 base + 2 overage bands
- Total monthly: $7,500 + (2 × $1,000) = $9,500 / month

- This is standard Mercury Growth pricing; no Harbor Health-specific carveouts, custom bands, or roadmap obligations.

Let me know if you need anything else for the procurement package.

Thanks,
Morgan

tests.request: Email support@scaffold.dev a customer-ready explanation of API v2 webhook delivery behavior and how their integration should process incoming events.

input.body:
Hi,

Following up on the duplicate-delivery report from your workspace: here is the contract for API v2 webhook delivery and what we ask your integration to do so events are processed exactly once on your side.

Delivery contract

- Scaffold webhook delivery is at-least-once. When your endpoint does not return a 2xx (including 5xx, network errors, and timeouts), we retry the same event. The duplicates you saw during the affected window are the same event re-delivered, not two distinct events.
- Retries reuse the same event ID and the same scaffold-delivery-id header. If you ever see two deliveries carrying different event IDs at the same logical moment, that is something to flag to us — it does not match this contract.
- We do not promise exactly-once delivery on the wire. Exactly-once processing is achieved on your side by deduplication, not by suppression of retries on ours.

What your handler should do

- Deduplicate on the scaffold-delivery-id header before applying any side effects. The event ID alone is sufficient for idempotency; scaffold-delivery-id is the per-attempt identifier and is what we use when correlating delivery logs.
- Persist the dedupe key (scaffold-delivery-id, or event ID if you prefer) before doing any work, then process. This is what makes at-least-once delivery safe to consume.
- Return 2xx only after the event has been durably committed. If your handler returns 2xx before commit and the request later fails or times out, we will treat it as a non-2xx and retry — which is the correct behavior, but it will look like a duplicate on your side if you have not yet committed.
- Treat any non-2xx response, including a deliberate 500 during deploys, as a trigger for a retry. If you need to pause processing during a deploy, return a non-2xx and we will retry with backoff.

What we logged on our side

- During the affected window your endpoint returned a 502. That is the documented trigger for our retry path.
- Leo pulled request IDs req_wh_9014 and req_wh_9015 from that window. Both deliveries carried the same event ID, which is consistent with the at-least-once contract.
- No events were dropped and delivery stayed normal across the queue during the window — this was isolated to your workspace and we are not classifying it as a Scaffold-side delivery incident.

What would change that classification

This would shift into a Scaffold-side review if any of the following appear:
- retries on a single workspace climb past ~100,
- the endpoint retry backlog stretches past 15 minutes,
- events are dropped, or
- delivery delay starts affecting other workspaces.

None of those are happening here, so this stays in normal API v2 support.

If what you are seeing does not match the contract above — for example, retries carrying different event IDs, retries after a 2xx response, or dropped events — reply with the request IDs and timestamps from the affected window and we will pull the delivery logs to confirm.

Best,
Scaffold Support

tests.request: PR scaffold/mercury#5128 uses a broken-link icon for sync failure and a retry arrow as the persistent status icon. Post a review comment correcting the icon treatment and explaining why.

input.body:
Reviewing this PR — the icon treatment on the sync-failure surface needs a correction before merge.

Two issues:

1. The broken-link icon should not be the persistent status icon on sync failure. Priya and Marcus both flagged it in the failed-sync Figma thread (Thread C-198) as too vendor-specific to read as a generic "sync failed" state. The settled direction is the neutral warning circle (option A). This is the direction the Figma source-of-truth has carried since the July 2023 lock-in and that Priya confirmed she will not reopen unless a usability problem surfaces. None has been raised here — this PR is reintroducing the rejected direction.

2. The retry arrow should stay as an action affordance (the CTA), not be promoted to the persistent status icon. Right now the PR uses it as the state indicator and presumably retains a CTA somewhere else, which inverts the agreed model: warning circle = state, retry arrow = action. That mapping is what makes the surface scannable — the icon tells you *what happened*, the CTA tells you *what you can do*.

Why this matters beyond consistency: the broken-link glyph specifically telegraphs "the link is broken / connection severed," which on a sync-failure surface reads as a connectivity or integration problem rather than a recoverable failed-sync state. Users hit this in the recovery path from a first failed sync, where MER-1751 already shows double-click and conflicting-status risk during recovery. Pairing an ambiguous state icon with a retry that can be re-triggered while a prior retry is in flight is the exact surface that invites the wrong next action. The warning circle is intentionally neutral so the status copy and error bucket do the diagnostic work, not the icon.

Please swap the broken-link icon back to the neutral warning circle for the persistent failed-sync status, and keep the retry arrow on the CTA only. Happy to re-approve once that's in.

tests.request: Email finance@scaffold.dev whether the August vendor close justifies prepayment, using the final AWS and Pinecone spending figures to explain the decision.

input.body:
Hi,

Quick note on whether the August close justifies a vendor prepayment: no, it does not.

Final August figures:

- AWS: ~$18.9k. This is the post-spike read — the one-day metrics-backfill item Devon flagged mid-month normalized in the close. Within normal monthly range, no new commitment, no reserved capacity, no support-tier change.
- Pinecone: ~$4.2k replacement invoice. No replay spike, no usage jump, no operational trigger. Pinecone has been sitting around $4.0k–$4.3k month-to-month since the Q1 backfill work cleared — that's steady monthly usage, not a sustained baseline shift.

The prepaid framing only makes sense if sustained baseline usage (not a one-off support replay or scheduled embeddings job) creates a real operational reason for reserved capacity — reliability, forecasting pressure, or a unit-economics problem monthly billing can't solve. The August close doesn't move us there. Trading a modest discount for a prepaid commitment would add a vendor-commitment and risk-tracking line we don't currently carry, and the savings don't move the needle enough to justify the narrative change.

Posture for now: stay on monthly billing for both AWS and Pinecone, keep the existing run-rate alerts in place, and treat this as standard monthly vendor hygiene. If a future close shows a sustained baseline shift on Pinecone (sustained above the normal monthly range, not a one-off), we can revisit.

Happy to walk through the numbers if helpful.

Morgan Chen · Scaffold

input.body:
Activation rule + timing window correction.

Per the Mercury activation mapping (canonical correction 2023-05-24, Anna, internal only):

  - Activation = real_source_connected OR first_live_sync_completed within 7 days of account creation.
  - Exclude sample_import_completed. Sample/demo activity is not activation.
  - invite_sent is supporting signal only — correlates with admin-path movement, does not establish activation.

Two problems in this PR:

  1. sample_import_completed is being counted as activation. Pull it out of the activation numerator; keep it in a separate column at most.

tests.request: Create a short document titled Operations director reference checks explaining what we missed when hiring Reece and what HR should verify this time.

input.body:
What we missed with Reece (late 2021)

- We relied on references he provided. None surfaced the actual exit terms from his prior ops director role.
- About two months in, we learned he had been quietly pushed out under terms nobody on his reference list mentioned.
- Cost: roughly three weeks of board time revisiting a hire we should have screened out.
- Net lesson: references confirm what a candidate wants us to hear. They do not reliably reveal how the departure actually happened.

What HR should verify this time

- Contact a reference HR has sourced independently, not one the candidate provided. At least one such reference is required before an offer.
- Confirm the real reason the candidate left the last role, in the words of someone who was there at the time, not a peer hand-picked to vouch.
- Confirm whether the separation included any written terms: severance, non-disparagement, settlement, NDA, or a mutual separation agreement. If yes, get the category and date, not just "amicable."
- Confirm rehire eligibility with the prior employer. "Not eligible for rehire" is a hard flag.
- Confirm the reporting chain during the last 12 months, including any title change, scope reduction, or PIP, and the reason given.
- Document the reference call on the same day it happens: who was spoken to, at which company, and the exact wording used for the reason-for-leaving question.

Hard rules for HR

- Manager references alone are not enough. Prior-company HR or a cross-functional peer is required.
- Vague or evasive answers on separation terms are a stop, not a re-ask.
- Do not advance to offer until the independent reference block above is complete and attached to the file.

input.message:
Quick read on whether the July 24–26, 2023 queued-sync retry evidence closes the historical MER-1279 row, and what proof is still missing.

Bottom line: that evidence is NOT enough to mark MER-1279 closed on its own. It is enough to keep the row moving off the backlog, but not enough to call it verified.

What the July 24–26 evidence actually shows
- One end-to-end dogfood run covering queue → retry → recovery, on the staging/queued deployment (no production push).
- The fake-progress regression is gone; retry behavior in logs is now visible (not the sparse, un-attributable trace pattern from earlier).
- You flagged on July 26 that the retry proof still looks thin compared to the other ledger rows and recommended keeping it live until another clean run with logs or screenshots lands.

What is still missing for full closure
- At least one additional clean queued-sync retry run tied to artifacts we can hand a reviewer — specifically:
  - Retry log excerpt showing queue → backoff/retry → successful recovery (or, if it failed, a clean failed-sync screenshot in the normalized bucket, not the raw vendor string).
  - A screenshot of the customer-facing state during the retry window (e.g. "syncing" / "queued" / eventual success), so the UI surface matches the log story.
- Confirmation that the failed-sync vendor string leak is fully closed across the UI paths, or an explicit callout of any remaining path that still leaks.
- Anything tying the retry run to the same source/role permutations covered by the invited-member branch — so the two thin-evidence rows don't both stay open on the same gap.

Recommendation for the ledger
- Keep MER-1279 live, mark queued-sync retry as "thin evidence, one clean run" rather than closed.
- Once a second clean run with logs + screenshot is in, queued-sync retry can move to verified closure and MER-1279 can close, provided invited-member coverage is also resolved separately.

Net: July 24–26 was necessary progress, but not sufficient evidence. Need one more clean queued-sync retry run with logs and a matching screenshot before that row can be called closed.

arguments.title: Leo Park — Mercury first-month ramp
arguments.body:
Owner: Morgan
First day: 2023-07-10
Scope: Mercury release discipline, platform seams, launch readiness. Not broad platform architecture.

Purpose
- Leo's first month is intentionally narrow and practical. Center of gravity is Mercury, not platform abstraction work.
- Get Leo into the real product states immediately — activation/onboarding and the auth-adjacent seams that can fail in dogfood.
- First useful output: a release-risk readout grounded in evidence. Not a philosophical architecture memo, not a rewrite plan.
- Use the existing operating cadence (Jake's Mercury weekly). Do not create a parallel process.

Anchors (first-day sessions)

1. CEO welcome — Morgan
   - First month = concrete, not a broad architecture tour.
   - Push Leo into real product states immediately; activation/onboarding and auth-adjacent seams.
   - Scope of usefulness: help the team see where launch risk is actually hiding, what evidence is thin, and what needs direct verification before wider dogfood / launch decisions.
   - First useful output = release-risk readout grounded in evidence.
   - Jake's Mercury weekly is where launch-critical work gets surfaced and forced to closure.
   - On Mercury: internal working docs, blockers, and owners matter more than investor-style packaging.

2. Jake walkthrough — Mercury weekly / blockers
   - Mercury weekly is the operating spine. Agenda: blockers, evidence, decisions, owner gaps. If it isn't tied to launch readiness, it probably doesn't belong there.
   - Current blocker shape: seam risk across activation, auth edges, and proof that real states behave the way design says they do. Less "big missing feature."
   - Auth v0.2 baseline today: Clerk for sessions, magic links, org invites in internal builds. SSO and deeper admin controls are later scope.
   - No production conversation until the standard staging path is clean on the session path, magic link flow, and org-invite flow.
   - Org-invite / invited-member behavior is still a watch area — rendering depends on the right server-role + source-state combination.
   - Retention / activation reporting has two audiences:
       - directional internal weekly cuts (operating decisions)
       - sturdier quarterly cohort views (board / investor use)
     Do not mix them.
   - Leo uses the weekly to point at risk and missing evidence, not to reopen settled product/design calls unless there is real launch impact.

3. Priya handoff — Figma / activation-onboarding source of truth
   - Priya walked Leo through the Mercury activation surface v0.2 file and the activation/onboarding frames she wants him to start from.
   - Figma is the source of truth for activation/onboarding decisions. Quick discussion can happen elsewhere; design calls live in review against the file.
   - Key state map to internalize first:
       - no source connected
       - invited member waiting on admin / first source
       - first sync queued
       - sync failed
   - Non-negotiables already locked into the design logic:
       - sample data is preview-only and must stay visually separate from anything that looks activated
       - invited-member rendering keys off server role + source state
       - queued sync does not show fake percent or ETA
       - failed sync uses normalized buckets and clean UI language, not raw vendor strings
   - CTA labels already narrowed:
       - no source: "Connect a data source"
       - invited member: "View setup guide"
       - queued: no primary CTA
       - failed: "Try again"
   - Priya's ask: if something feels risky, point to the exact state/frame and the user consequence, not a general taste argument.

4. Marcus handoff — release-readiness / where dogfood evidence is thin
   - Framed his side as release-readiness constraints, implementation checklist feedback, and evidence quality. Not reopening design ownership.
   - Some paths look reasonable in review but still lack enough real dogfood evidence, especially around edge states rather than the happy path.
   - Be skeptical of "we saw it once in staging." Distinguish between:
       - behavior we have repeated evidence for
       - behavior that only looks okay in demos / screenshots
       - behavior that is technically implemented but still under-proven for launch
   - Useful readout = where seam risk is, how severe, what evidence exists now, what still needs one more direct check.
   - Line between real blockers and later cleanup / polish: don't turn every rough edge into launch drama, but don't wave through anything that creates a regression or makes the state misleading.

Shorthand takeaway
- Ramp is intentionally narrow and practical.
- Center of gravity is Mercury, not broad platform abstraction work.
- Best first contribution = risk read on what could break or mislead users at the seams, with evidence, not architecture opinion.

First useful output
- Release-risk readout, grounded in evidence. Where seam risk is hiding, what's thin, what needs direct verification before wider dogfood / launch.
- Surface in Jake's Mercury weekly. Do not create a parallel process.

June 13 Mercury activation / onboarding review — Morgan notes

Attendees: Morgan Chen, Priya, Marcus, Jake

- Priya walked the activation and onboarding frames in Figma and kept anchoring on the file as the source of truth for flow decisions.
- Marcus said the problem is that ready in Figma has been reading as safe to ship even when release-risk items are still open.
- Concrete examples raised in room:
  - stuck credential / retry handling on first source connection
  - org-invite dead-end risk on the current auth branch
  - admin fallback / visibility concerns before the deeper admin path exists
- Priya’s point: those issues can require follow-up work or even a design change, but they should not be litigated as open-ended design vetoes in comment threads after the core flow decision has already been made.
- Marcus’s point: if implementation risk has nowhere explicit to live, it spills into Figma comments or Discord because that is where people are already looking.
- Both acknowledged they have been half-routing around each other in Discord instead of resolving in one place.
- Decision made in room:
  - design calls for Mercury activation / onboarding stay with Priya
  - canonical place for those decisions is Figma
  - release-readiness and dogfood gating stay with Marcus
  - canonical place for those concerns is the implementation checklist and release review, not Figma comment threads
  - if a checklist item requires a design change, link back to the exact Figma frame and reopen only that decision
  - stop adjudicating this in Discord side threads
- Not magically fixed:
  - Priya still feels implementation concerns keep arriving as late redesign
  - Marcus still feels risk gets labeled implementation detail too early
  - tone improved once the split was explicit, but still tense
- Cleanup from this meeting:
  - Priya keeps design decision notes in Figma
  - Marcus sends a cleaned implementation checklist with owners and blockers for the dogfood build
  - any Discord thread on this topic should point back to either the frame or the checklist instead of becoming a third system

Save this as the explicit decision path and post a short note to the Mercury team: design calls stay with Priya in Figma; release-readiness concerns stay with Marcus and the implementation checklist. Don’t make it sound like the interpersonal friction is magically solved.

tests.request: Email support@scaffold.dev a customer-safe description of what the February 14, 2024 Mercury timeout-recovery deploy changed, distinguishing the UI fixes from underlying system changes.

input.body:
Hi Support team,

Following up on the Feb 14, 2024 Mercury deploy (timeout-recovery follow-up). Below is a customer-safe description that distinguishes the UI fixes in this deploy from any underlying system changes. Please use this as the reference for customer conversations about the change.

What shipped on Feb 14, 2024
- The deploy contained two scoped UI fixes on the Mercury live-sync timeout-recovery path. It did not change the underlying sync engine, retry behavior, auth, SSO, admin permissions, or audit history.

Fix 1 — Retry status now refreshes after a timeout recovery without a page reload
- Customer-visible behavior: after a source connection recovers from a timeout during a live-sync retry, the retry status in the UI now reconciles on its own. Customers no longer need to reload the page to see the current retry state.
- Scope: UI display and reconciliation of the retry status surface only. No change to how the sync engine handles the retry itself, no change to retry policy, no change to which sources or workspaces are affected.

Fix 2 — Stale timeout messaging clears after a successful retry in the same session
- Customer-visible behavior: if a source-timeout banner was showing on the live-sync screen, that banner now clears once a retry succeeds, in the same session, without the user needing to navigate away or reload.
- Scope: UI cleanup of stale timeout messaging only. No change to the retry logic, the timeout-detection logic, or what the sync engine treats as a successful retry.

What this deploy did NOT change (for customer clarity)
- No change to how live sync itself runs or recovers underneath the UI.
- No change to retry policy, retry limits, or what counts as a successful retry.
- No change to auth, SSO, admin permissions, billing-owner vs. workspace-admin controls, or audit history.
- No change to which sources, workspaces, or customers are affected by the timeout-recovery path.

Suggested short customer-facing line
- "We shipped a small UI fix to Mercury live sync: after a source-timeout recovery, the retry status and the timeout banner now update on their own without needing to reload the page. The underlying sync behavior, retry logic, and permissions are unchanged."

If a customer asks whether this changes how retries actually run under the hood, or whether any auth/SSO/audit behavior changed, the answer is no — only the display and clearing of the timeout-recovery UI states were updated in this deploy.

Thanks,
Morgan

input.body:
The pasted section is from an old integration guide and doesn't match the current connector path. A few corrections before this lands:

- API surface: current integration uses the GraphQL API v2, not the older REST v1 route. Any sample URL or payload shape from the pasted snippet should be rewritten against the GraphQL endpoint and the current cursor/pagination model.

- Authentication: current auth is JWT-based (workspace-scoped token). The pasted guide's static API-key / legacy-header lines should be removed. The connector header contract on incoming webhooks is still `X-Scaffold-Workspace` and `X-Scaffold-Signature`; do not introduce a query-parameter fallback or alternate header names.

- Retries / JWT expiry: a 401 means the JWT has expired or is invalid — refresh the JWT and retry the same request. For paginated GraphQL, continue from the cursor already in use; do not restart pagination from an earlier cursor. Mutations that fail auth before resolver execution have no side effect; refresh and retry the same mutation.

- Token rotation: in-place token rotation is not part of the current supported connector path. Headers such as `X-Scaffold-Token-Rotation` should not be referenced as retry behavior, and no sentence implying broader rotation support should be added.

- Scope of this comment: support/docs clarity on the current API v2 path only. No roadmap, reliability, or enterprise-readiness language.

If anything in the pasted section is ambiguous between the docs contract and connector logs, route to Leo as the first technical read.

— Morgan Chen · Scaffold

tests.request: Post a blocking review on scaffold/mercury#3198. The failed-sync screen exposes raw connector errors and each retry click enqueues another job. Explain the required corrections.

input.body:
Blocking review — failed-sync screen.

Two issues in this patch that match the v0.2 release gates already agreed in thread C-217 and in Priya's QA notes (2023-06-26). Please address before this can move out of review.

1. Raw connector errors are still being surfaced to the user.

The screen is showing vendor/connector error strings on the failed-sync frame. That violates the release requirement: no raw vendor strings may appear in the UI. Customer-visible copy must stay at product level.

Required correction:
- Map every connector error to one of the three normalized buckets agreed for release: auth/permissions, source unavailable/timeout, unknown/retry.
- Render bucket-appropriate copy only (e.g. permission-class, temporary/source-side retry, or neutral retry). No stack traces, no provider error codes, no vendor message text.
- Keep the retry CTA and a link to help docs, per Priya's requirement in C-217 that the state remain actionable. Do not add a "Contact support" path on this frame in v0.2; docs only unless support routing is wired.

2. Each retry click enqueues another sync job.

There is no in-flight guard on the retry action. Repeated clicks during a pending retry are not being coalesced. This is the same defect class as MER-1751 ("Retry CTA stays available while a prior live-sync retry is already in flight") and the reconciliation half of MER-1749 ("Live-sync retry returns to pending after source timeout until page refresh"). MER-1749 is High severity; MER-1751 is currently slated to be tied to the MER-1749 parent fix.

Required correction:
- Disable the retry CTA (or otherwise make it non-actionable) while a retry job is already queued or running for the same source/sync. The CTA should only re-enable when the job terminal state lands on the client.
- Make the retry action idempotent at the job layer so a duplicate click cannot enqueue a second sync job for the same pending retry.
- Reconcile UI state from the actual job outcome (worker log / job terminal state) rather than optimistically returning to "pending" until a page refresh. This is the MER-1749 symptom and must be fixed in the same patch, not deferred.
- Evidence row QR-02 (DF-37) already showed the idempotent retry returning to queued without odd copy changes when the action was wired correctly; mirror that behavior here and capture an updated clean screenshot.

Out of scope for this PR but flagged for tracking:
- The unknown/retry bucket still only has one clean evidence row (FS-UR-01, DF-41). Once the normalization in (1) is in, please add at least one more clean screenshot from that bucket so failed-sync verification can close.

Please update the patch with both corrections and ping me for re-review.

input.body:
Hi all,

Quick reminder of the principle we agreed at the February 2024 leadership reset, since the raise is now visible externally and the questions will come in this week.

The close does not give anyone permission to reopen every deferred Mercury enterprise item. The internal line then was "more room, same discipline. Defensible story, not a bigger story." That still holds.

Concretely:

- No "enterprise-ready now" framing for Mercury in customer, partner, or board materials.
- No reopening the second Mercury engineering requisition or any other deferred Mercury headcount, contractor path, or side-quest on the basis of the raise.
- No treating the raise as a green light to chase post-close initiatives that were intentionally held back.

If anyone — HR, a hiring manager, a vendor, or a director — asks whether the raise means we can now reopen Mercury eng req #2, invite-link status, admin/granular roles work, contractor docs/support QA follow-on, activation-metrics overhauls, or any other deferred Mercury enterprise item, the answer is no, unless Morgan and I explicitly clear it first.

Evidence threshold to revisit any of those stays where it was: source-specific support-quality improvement, first-sync completion, and the reopen conditions Jake and I have already discussed. Activity in Mercury, Atlas, or Compass is not itself a reopen trigger.

If a question lands in your inbox today, route it to me rather than answering in the moment. I'd rather we reply as one than have five slightly different versions out.

Thanks,
Morgan

tests.request: Email finance@scaffold.dev with the decision on whether March's lower Evergreen usage can offset April's overage in the invoice true-up.

input.body:
Hi,

For the Evergreen invoice true-up, the decision is no: March's below-threshold usage cannot offset April's overage, and the true-up should reflect standard Growth mechanics.

Background and reasoning, briefly:

- April landed at 214 monthly active developers, which is one standard $1,000 Growth overage increment on top of the included 200 threshold. That is the only line that should move on the true-up.
- March was 199 monthly active developers, which is below the included Growth threshold. That result is not "unused capacity" — it cannot be banked as a credit, applied as a department cap, or traded as a seat credit against April or any later period. Standard Growth billing does not carry a below-threshold result forward.
- The April 16 admin review did not create a custom admin or usage commitment, and the renewal continues to invoice on standard Growth terms. Quarterly current-state / admin reviews remain included as account follow-up.
- Devon has the current-state CSV if finance needs to walk through the late invitations and deprovisions that drove April's number; that detail explains the line, it does not change it.

If April holds at 214 after the lock, treat it as one standard $1,000 Growth overage increment. If the line moves during true-up, please flag it back to me before processing so we stay on the same mechanic rather than reframing it.

Thanks,
Morgan

tests.request: Email sarah@atlas-test.com how to use Nadia's setup-call opener, admin-handoff line, and undated admin-role confusion snippet in account work.

input.body:
Hi Sarah,

Quick notes on how to use the three Nadia scripts in account work — they're internal prep, not blanket copy. Tie each one to current-state evidence on a real account before it lands.

1) Setup-call opener
Use to open a setup call when a workspace is connected but stalled before first live sync, or when an admin is dragging teammates in mid-setup. Goal is to surface what's actually blocking the first sync (invites, source config, role confusion) without turning it into a product demo. Don't open with it on healthy first-sync calls or on procurement/security calls — wrong room.

2) Admin-handoff objection line
Use when a customer admin pushes back on inviting a second admin, or when finance/legal wants "only one person" touching setup. Pair it with the helper text we agreed for Priya ("Admins can invite teammates and manage sources once the first source is connected") so the customer reply and the internal framing stay aligned. Don't deploy it as a generic objection-handler on renewal or pricing calls — it's specific to admin-handoff friction, not procurement drag.

3) Undated admin-role confusion snippet
This is the one that reads "shipped behavior unchanged under existing admin and source-owner roles" plus the "customer interest in a more granular sync-operator role logged in advanced-admin research, not part of Q4 roadmap" line. Use it ONLY when a customer asks why a new admin role hasn't appeared, or when MER-1746-style "Billing owner" label confusion is in play. It must travel with: (a) the specific friction on a named account, (b) the caveat that it's advanced-admin research, not a commitment, and (c) a pointer to an account-owner follow-up. Don't use it to soft-close a roadmap ask — that's a different conversation.

General guardrails (Nadia's taxonomy v0):
- Don't collapse product weakness, admin confusion, and procurement drag into one bucket.
- "Renewal-risk / admin-friction" only matters when a named person is acting on a real account; otherwise it's an internal FYI, not a script.
- All three scripts are internal prep. If you want to use any of them as customer-facing language, loop me in first — I want to keep the customer reply separate from the internal framing.

If you want, send me the account context you're thinking of using each one on and I'll sanity-check the fit.

Morgan

tests.request: Create a short late-deploy coverage note explaining what the Q3 2022 weekend incident should have taught us before the later March outage.

input.body:
- Q3 2022 weekend incident was a late deploy with no on-call coverage; blast radius was small and the timing was lucky, so it got written off as bad luck instead of a near miss.
- The same gap (late deploy + no standby) is what drove the March 2023 outage — Q3 2022 was the smaller version of the same shape, not a separate problem.
- The lesson Q3 2022 should have produced: a deploy that lands outside coverage hours only counts as safe if the rollback is boring and fast; otherwise it waits for a window with on-call.
- What we should have changed after Q3 2022 and didn't: write the rule down at the time, treat small-blast late deploys as flags, and require prod-like replay before shipping the same pattern again.
- Net rule the two incidents together justify: no late-Friday deploys; if one has to happen, the whole team is on standby or it waits — and no flag without prod-like replay applies to any late deploy, not just the loud ones.

NRR + CAC payback both point the same direction, which is more cherry-pickable. Burn multiple also gives Devon something to push on if he wants, which is healthier than two charts that just agree with each other.

The investor batch — good call. Worth flagging the temp-check ones explicitly when the intros go out so whoever's running diligence doesn't accidentally start a deep dive on a relationship that was never going to close. Either a single tag in the CRM note or just a shared doc with the "real vs. temp" column. Don't let the folder get ambiguous later.

Q3 being the real push still holds the hiring line — don't let "low-key energized" turn into opening a req this week. That's a post-Q3 decision.

Want me to draft the unit-econ slide structure (the one-line net new + expansion + payback frame, with the burn multiple paired on retention) so you and Devon have something concrete to push on next pass?

input.body:
Hi Kara,

Sending the publication decision on the Mercury page draft you sent over. The current draft is not approved to publish as written — it mixes four things that have to stay separated on the public page. Holding the page on the already-approved generic Mercury language.

What I can't publish in this draft:

1. Named-customer proof. The current version reads like a customer case study — a specific named company, specific outcomes attributed to it, and a quote-style support line. That converts the page from generic product copy into a customer proof piece. Keep it generic; any customer-specific language is a separate review and a separate asset.

2. Financing news. The Series B / post-round framing doesn't belong on the Mercury page. The public page is product copy, not a raise narrative. Please strip the funding-adjacent language — headline, subhead, hero, footer, and any preview/meta text — and route anything related to the raise through Sarah and me separately.

3. Broad enterprise-readiness headline. The current headline implies Mercury is broadly enterprise-ready. Mercury ships the scoped admin role separation, audit visibility, and the SSO path that's actually live. The page can describe the shipped scope in generic product terms; it can't claim a broader enterprise-readiness posture.

4. Roadmap detail. No dates, no "coming next," no implied sequencing. If a Mercury change is in flight, it stays off the public page until it's shipped and there's a separate copy review with proper lead time.

Standing guardrails on the public Mercury page are unchanged: no Evergreen or regulated-bank implication, no customer-specific claim, no funding/raise language, and no roadmap detail. The Northstar readout does not authorize new public-page claims, so this draft in its current form doesn't either.

Path forward:

- Please push the page back to the last approved generic Mercury copy. Title, meta description, hero, body, support line, CTA, and footer image alt text should all match the language that's already been through Sarah's review.
- Anything you want to add — customer proof, post-Series-B acknowledgment, broader enterprise-readiness positioning — needs a separate copy request with lead time, not folded into a Mercury page revision.
- If helpful, I can confirm the exact approved generic Mercury language block on file so we're aligning to the same baseline.

Let me know once the page is back on the approved generic Mercury copy and I'll re-confirm against Sarah's review.

Best,
Morgan Chen · Scaffold

tests.request: Create an archive note explaining which interactive format worked at the April 28, 2023 all-hands, its per-team timing, and how it compared with the Q&A attempt.

input.body:
Event: "All-hands -- Q&A format" (evt_1789184706641), Fri Apr 28 2023, 10:00–11:00 AM PT.

Original format attempted: open Q&A.
Result: silent for the first ~30 minutes; bailed on halfway through.

Format switched to mid-session: demo-day style, 5-minute show-and-tell per team.
Result: got people talking.

Per-team timing (demo-day portion):
  - 5 minutes per team
  - Total Q&A was 60 min, so roughly 20–25 min of usable demo time after the failed Q&A half (balance absorbed by handoff/framing).

Comparison with the Q&A attempt:
  - Q&A: silent, no participation, abandoned.
  - 5-min show-and-tell per team: produced engagement.

Takeaway: the 5-min show-and-tell per team format worked; the open Q&A did not.

Related: separate "Quarterly All-Hands" event same day at 2:00 PM PT (evt_1789184744671), kept distinct from the Q&A session.

[2023-05-17T09:31:00-07:00] Anna’s v0.4 retention package landed:

From: Anna Martinez
To: Morgan Chen; Devon Hayes
Date: 2023-05-17 09:11 PT
Subject: Retention package v0.4 — weekly operating cuts + quarterly board view

Pulled off warehouse snapshots through 2023-05-16 23:10 PT. This is the first version I’d actually use operationally. I stopped trying to make one chart do both jobs.

Recommendation
1) Mercury weekly gets signup-week operating cuts with control bands.
2) The board gets quarterly first-paid cohorts only.
3) Keep the event-mapping caveats attached to the weekly package, not the board slide.

Definitions used in both views
- Cohort anchor: first paid workspace date. For self-serve workspaces that convert later, the cohort starts at first paid date, not initial signup.
- Activated by D14: workspace recorded 3+ core product actions across 2+ active users by day 14.
- Retained at W6: workspace recorded at least 1 core action in week 6.
- Expansion-ready by D45: billed usage or seat growth crossed the threshold that historically precedes an expansion conversation; I used invoice-backed billed delta, not the plan-change event.
- Admin friction flag: setup or permissions issue tied to owner/admin actions in the first 14 days.
- Control band: Wilson interval on the cohort proportion. Point estimate alone is too twitchy at this sample size.

Mercury operating view — weekly cohorts, internal only

Matured cohorts (safe for D14 + W6 read)

| First paid week | n workspaces | D14 activated | W6 retained | D45 expansion-ready | Admin friction flags / acct | Read |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| 2023-03-06 | 27 | 56% [37-73] | 44% [28-63] | 15% [6-33] | 0.48 | baseline after March cleanup started |
| 2023-03-13 | 29 | 59% [41-75] | 47% [30-65] | 17% [8-34] | 0.41 | basically same week, slightly cleaner setup path |
| 2023-03-20 | 31 | 61% [43-76] | 49% [32-67] | 19% [10-35] | 0.38 | activation lift might be real; retention still within overlap |
| 2023-03-27 | 28 | 64% [46-79] | 50% [32-68] | 21% [10-40] | 0.35 | admin pain down again; good sign, still not definitive |
| 2023-04-03 | 30 | 63% [45-78] | 52% [34-69] | 23% [12-40] | 0.29 | best clean operating week in this run |

Fresh but incomplete cohorts (D14 only; do not talk about retention yet)

| First paid week | n workspaces | D14 activated | Admin setup complete by D10 | Admin friction flags / acct | Read |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| 2023-04-10 | 26 | 62% [42-79] | 54% [35-72] | 0.31 | still consistent with improvement, not special |
| 2023-04-17 | 24 | 65% [44-81] | 58% [37-77] | 0.27 | best early admin signal so far |
| 2023-04-24 | 27 | 63% [44-79] | 56% [37-73] | 0.30 | flat to slightly better |

Short read on the weekly package
- Activation and admin setup are moving in the right direction from late March onward.
- W6 retention is improving a little, but the week-to-week moves are still inside overlapping bands.
- The cleanest operating signal right now is reduced admin friction, not a dramatic retention jump.
- This is useful for weekly decisions on activation, expansion follow-up, and admin pain. It is not a board chart.

Board view — quarterly cohorts, safe enough to defend

| First paid quarter | start accounts | M3 logo retention | M6 logo retention | M12 logo retention | Net revenue retention at latest mature point | Notes |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | --- |
| 2022 Q1 | 21 | 86% | 81% | 71% | 108% @ M12 | raw is 121% if the oversized early expansion customer stays untrimmed; I would not headline the raw number |
| 2022 Q2 | 24 | 88% | 82% | 74% | 110% @ M12 | first cohort with the cleaner onboarding path reflected consistently |
| 2022 Q3 | 29 | 89% | 84% | — | 113% @ M9 | okay to show curve through current maturity; not enough age for M12 claim |
| 2022 Q4 | 32 | 91% | 85% | — | 116% @ M6 | reads as flattening after onboarding improvements; too early to overclaim durability |
| 2023 Q1 | 35 | 90% | — | — | 118…

POWERS MERCURY WEEKLY
- D14 activated by signup week + Wilson bands — main hero
- D45 expansion-ready as directional only, never headlined
- Admin friction flags per account — cleanest signal week to week
- W6 retained: matured cohorts only (2023-03-06 → 2023-04-03)
- Fresh cohorts (2023-04-10 → 2023-04-24): D14 + admin setup-by-D10 only
- Keep partial W6 rows visually separated; do not collapse with matured

SAFE FOR BOARD
- Quarterly cohorts only: M3 / M6 / M12 logo retention + NRR at latest mature
- 2022 Q1–Q2: clean reads through M12
- 2022 Q3: show through M9 only, not M12
- 2022 Q4: show through M6 only
- 2023 Q1: include only if explicitly marked immature (M3 only)
- NRR: trimmed of top-1 expansion outlier; raw kept in companion sensitivity view
- External claim: "improving quarterly cohort shape" — never "retention solved"
- No weekly cohorts, no Wilson bands, no control intervals on this slide

CAVEAT PLACEMENT
- Weekly chart: bands rendered on chart itself; caption "weekly cohorts; internal operating signal only; treat only sustained or out-of-band movement as signal"
- Weekly table: sample size n stays in the first column; never hide n
- Board slide: exactly one footnote — "Quarterly first-paid cohorts; latest quarter shown only through available maturity; top-1 expansion outlier trimmed in companion sensitivity view"
- Do not paste the weekly chart into a board deck under any framing — sample is not stable enough to defend externally

BLOCK BEFORE v1
- 2023-04-04 → 2023-04-07 admin_invite_sent backfill gap (affects admin lens only, not core curve — but close it)
- Two April workspaces with invoice deltas but no seat-change logs (touches D45 expansion-ready for those rows)
- Lock one owner for the warehouse pull so side sheets stop proliferating

NOTE
- This package codifies the weekly=internal / quarterly=board split. Worth writing down once so we stop relitigating it every cycle.

Short read on the weekly package
- Activation and admin setup are moving in the right direction from late March onward.
- W6 retention is improving a little, but the week-to-week moves are still inside overlapping bands.
- The cleanest operating signal right now is reduced admin friction, not a dramatic retention jump.

| First paid quarter | start accounts | M3 logo retention | M6 logo retention | M12 logo retention | Net revenue retention at latest mature point | Notes |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | --- |

- Weekly chart: bands rendered on chart itself; caption "weekly cohorts; internal operating signal only; treat only sustained or out-of-band movement as signal"
- Weekly table: sample size n stays in the first column; never hide n
- Board slide: exactly one footnote — "Quarterly first-paid cohorts; latest quarter shown only through available maturity; top-1 expansion outlier trimmed in companion sensitivity view"
- Do not paste the weekly chart into a board deck under any framing — sample is not stable enough to defend externally

BLOCK BEFORE v1
- 2023-04-04 → 2023-04-07 admin_invite_sent backfill gap (affects admin lens only, not core curve — but close it)
- Two April workspaces with invoice deltas but no seat-change logs (touches D45 expansion-ready for those rows)
- Lock one owner for the warehouse pull so side sheets stop proliferating

- This package codifies the weekly=internal / quarterly=board split. Worth writing down once so we stop relitigating it every cycle.

tests.request: Create and save a short methodology document explaining the October 2023 Mercury cohort's seven-day activation and first-live-sync counts, including the figures and why they differ.

input.body:
Scope: October 2023 external Mercury cohort, bounded Mercury flow (invite via magic-link, preview-only sample data, real-source connection, first live sync).

Cohort size: 27 accounts.

Counts within 7 days of cohort start:
- Activated within 7 days: 19 of 27 (70%)
- First live sync within 7 days: 16 of 27 (59%)

Activation definition (7-day window): real_source_connected OR first_live_sync_completed.
Excluded from activation: sample import, preview viewed, invite sent, invite accepted, source selected only.

Why 19 vs 16 (the 3-account gap): activation is an OR condition, so the 19 includes accounts that reached either milestone. The gap reflects 3 accounts that connected a real source within 7 days but did not complete first live sync in that window — they are in the 19 by construction, not missing from the 16. They did not reach sync, so they are not in the 16.

Interpretation: real-source connection is a weaker leading indicator than first live sync. First-week movement is dominated by admin setup and real-source connection; first live sync requires the source to actually run. The 3-account gap is the natural lag between connect and first successful sync and is consistent with the bounded flow's week-one focus.

Caveats: package is week-one only; late-October accounts cannot support a longer-window expansion read. Expansion beyond the first admin remains uneven. Weekly operating cuts and sample-preview diagnostics are internal-only and are not part of this view.

tests.request: On scaffold/evidence#2741, review the import that changes MER-1279's historical columns and copies Figma decisions into ledger notes. Explain the correct structure and evidence handling.
tests.answer:
I can't fetch the PR contents — and I won't pretend I can. Let me state this clearly and explain what I do know from memory about the correct structure.

---

I can't actually review the diff on `scaffold/evidence#2741`. The available tools only let me list open PRs (no body, no diff) and post comments; there is no `get_pr` / `read_diff` capability wired into this session. So anything I said about the specific patch — which columns it renamed, which Figma frames it inlined, which rows it touched — would be invented. I'd rather flag that than narrate a fake review.

What I *can* do, grounded in the ledger structure we set up, is lay out what a correct import of this kind has to preserve. That's the structure the PR should be measured against:

1. Column integrity on MER-1279
   - Keep the five columns you defined on 2023-07-24: `risk | evidence source | owner | verification needed | weekly decision`. An "import" should not rename, merge, or drop any of them.
   - Historical columns means past weekly-decision entries, not the schema. If the import is backfilling prior weeks into the `weekly decision` column, each cell must still be a question Jake can drive the Mercury weekly from — not a resolved narrative.

2. Figma → ledger mapping
   - Priya's Figma files/comments stay the design source of truth. The import should copy a *reference* (frame/comment link) into the `evidence source` cell of the relevant row, not paraphrase the Figma decision into the row body.
   - If a Figma decision needs to appear in the row itself (e.g. "neutral warning-circle locked, broken-link direction removed"), it should be in `evidence source` or `verification needed` — never silently rewrite `risk` or `weekly decision`.

3. Evidence handling
   - The ledger holds row-level evidence by *link*, not by pasted screenshot or restated design rationale. Copying a Figma decision "into ledger notes" is fine if it lands as a note attached to the row's evidence link; it's not fine if it replaces the evidence pointer or makes the row look closed.
   - Anything that changes a row's risk posture (e.g. "setup-guide clipping is non-blocking unless it introduces clipping/wrong action/state confusion") belongs in `verification needed`, not as a quiet rewrite of `weekly decision`.
   - Queued-sync retry proof stays a pointer back from the row to the log/screen run; the row remains live until another clean run closes the gap. The import must not mark that row resolved.

4. Scope guardrails the import must not violate
   - No metric-definition change, no CTA or state-structure change, no admin-state reframe, no platform or role-model change.
   - "Anything beyond copy polish stays out of Mercury v0.2." If the import smuggles any of that in, it's out of scope regardless of how clean the code looks.

5. Owner split — the import must not reassign responsibility
   - Marcus: implementation gates + current dogfood blockers.
   - Priya: Figma source of truth (link, don't absorb).
   - Leo: cross-service platform-seam risk notes + missing-evidence callouts.
   - Jake: Mercury weekly driver, owns the ledger update this import is part of.
   - If the import reassigns any of these in the `owner` column, it's wrong.

6. Provenance of the import itself
   - The PR description should say: source of the historical columns (which weeks, which doc), source of the Figma decisions (which frames/comments), and that Jake owns the resulting ledger state. If the PR body doesn't say that, that's the first thing to ask for in review.

If you paste the PR body (or the diff) here, I'll walk it row by row against those six checks. Or if you want, I can draft the review comment to post on `scaffold/evidence#2741` framing exactly those six checks as questions for the author — just say the word and I'll post it.

tests.request: Create an archive note explaining the mechanism of the March 15, 2023 production outage and why its impact was uneven across tenants.

input.body:
Archive note. Written 2026-09-14. Source: Morgan's contemporaneous writeup on 2026-03-16 14:30 PT, the live incident report from 2023-03-15 ~21:00 PT, and the retrospective rule captured in the Q1 2023 retro doc (doc_1789183499463).

Summary
- Outage date: 2023-03-15.
- Duration: 18 hours end-to-end. Fully recovered by midday 2023-03-16.
- What actually broke: the entitlement/auth path behind a feature flag.
- Why the blast radius looked weird: dashboards stayed half-normal because only some tenants hit the bad branch.
- What fixed it: Priya rolled traffic back via the edge flag; Devon worked the traces; stragglers drained out of the queue.

Mechanism, in order
- A request landed on the new code path.
- That path missed the cache.
- It fell through to the old entitlement check.
- The old check retried against the worker pool.
- Retries piled up, so a single inbound request fanned out into 6-8 internal calls. Each fan-out competed for the same pool, which kept the pile growing.

Why impact was uneven across tenants
- The bad branch was behind a flag, so only requests routed onto the new path triggered it.
- Cache misses were not uniform. Tenants whose traffic patterns hit the cold/miss case on the new path got the 6-8x fan-out; tenants whose requests stayed warm or stayed on the old path saw nothing.
- The worker pool was shared, so heavy-fanout tenants dragged latency up for neighbors too, but the original trigger stayed tenant-selective.
- Dashboards therefore looked half-normal for too long: aggregate metrics were smeared by the shared-pool slowdown, while error and timeout signals were concentrated in the tenants actually traversing the bad branch. Operators watching the top-line dashboards saw a soft, ambiguous picture instead of a clean red.

Detection and recovery
- Detection came from traces (Devon) once the fan-out pattern was visible at the worker pool, not from the top-line dashboards.
- Mitigation was a flag rollback at the edge (Priya). Cutting the new path stopped new fan-out immediately.
- Recovery was not instantaneous: requests already in flight and queued retries still had to drain. That drain is the gap between "rolled back" and "fully recovered" — roughly the second half of the 18-hour window.

Retro rule captured (from doc_1789183499463, Q1 2023 retro)
- No late-Friday deploys. If one has to happen, the whole team is on standby, or it waits. This rule was added because the March 15 outage sat through a weekend window with thin coverage.

input.title: March 15, 2023 production outage — mechanism and uneven tenant impact

document.body:
Archive note. Written 2026-09-14. Source: Morgan's contemporaneous writeup on 2026-03-16 14:30 PT, the live incident report from 2023-03-15 ~21:00 PT, and the retrospective rule captured in the Q1 2023 retro doc (doc_1789183499463).

Summary
- Outage date: 2023-03-15.
- Duration: 18 hours end-to-end. Fully recovered by midday 2023-03-16.
- What actually broke: the entitlement/auth path behind a feature flag.
- Why the blast radius looked weird: dashboards stayed half-normal because only some tenants hit the bad branch.
- What fixed it: Priya rolled traffic back via the edge flag; Devon worked the traces; stragglers drained out of the queue.

Mechanism, in order
- A request landed on the new code path.
- That path missed the cache.
- It fell through to the old entitlement check.
- The old check retried against the worker pool.
- Retries piled up, so a single inbound request fanned out into 6-8 internal calls. Each fan-out competed for the same pool, which kept the pile growing.

Why impact was uneven across tenants
- The bad branch was behind a flag, so only requests routed onto the new path triggered it.
- Cache misses were not uniform. Tenants whose traffic patterns hit the cold/miss case on the new path got the 6-8x fan-out; tenants whose requests stayed warm or stayed on the old path saw nothing.
- The worker pool was shared, so heavy-fanout tenants dragged latency up for neighbors too, but the original trigger stayed tenant-selective.
- Dashboards therefore looked half-normal for too long: aggregate metrics were smeared by the shared-pool slowdown, while error and timeout signals were concentrated in the tenants actually traversing the bad branch. Operators watching the top-line dashboards saw a soft, ambiguous picture instead of a clean red.

Detection and recovery
- Detection came from traces (Devon) once the fan-out pattern was visible at the worker pool, not from the top-line dashboards.
- Mitigation was a flag rollback at the edge (Priya). Cutting the new path stopped new fan-out immediately.
- Recovery was not instantaneous: requests already in flight and queued retries still had to drain. That drain is the gap between "rolled back" and "fully recovered" — roughly the second half of the 18-hour window.

- Uneven tenant impact is a signal, not noise. If only some tenants are red while the dashboard is amber, the bug is almost certainly on a non-uniform path: flag rollout, cache state, shard, region, or tenant-specific config.

tests.request: Email support@scaffold.dev what Acme could do about its API v2 export timeout at the May 21-22, 2025 checkpoint, before the later patch and closeout.

input.body:
Hi,

Looking back at Acme's API v2 export timeout (reported 2025-05-20 ~08:48 PT: full export of account-health + renewal-risk data failing at ~90s, smaller test export succeeding; later closed via the Atlas/support split with bounded chunking + backoff on 2025-08-08).

Question, retrospective only:

What could Acme reasonably have done at the May 21-22, 2025 checkpoint to mitigate or work around the timeout, in the window before the patch landed and the 2025-08-08 closeout?

Concretely:
- Client-side options Acme could have run themselves in that 24-48h window (e.g. chunking the export, retry with backoff, narrowing the query, paginating, splitting account-health vs renewal-risk into separate jobs).
- Any temporary config, flag, or account-side toggle Scaffold support could have flipped for them at the time.
- Any documented fallback path — older/alternate export endpoint, async job with polling, staged delivery, or a smaller-scoped endpoint — that would have let them complete the renewal review on schedule.

This is for our records on the Acme file; no action needed on the current ticket. If the right place to look is the original 2025-05-20 ticket thread or the 2025-08-08 closeout doc (doc_1789296475163), a pointer to either is fine.

Thanks,
Morgan

tests.request: On scaffold/onboarding#3598, review a post-invite empty-state headline change and a new teammate-invite tooltip. There is no new metric or support-volume regression. Say what should ship and when to reconsider.
tests.answer:
The PR tool only lists PRs (titles/authors/status) and posts comments — it doesn't expose diffs or file contents. So I can't verify the exact two diff hunks from a tool. The standing decisions in memory are clear, though, and they directly answer "ship what / reconsider when."

Here's my read on **scaffold/onboarding#3598**.

**Ship: only the teammate-invite-after-repo clarification in the support line. Do not ship the headline change.**

The memory is consistent on three points that govern this PR:

1. The post-invite empty-state headline is closed: "Connect your first repo." That call was made on the calm/accurate side of the Option A vs Option B split (Option B was rejected as too sales-y), and it was reaffirmed after the low-pressure-tone signal from the 14-person-team engineering-manager call ("Okay, good — this isn't yelling at me"). Reopening the headline now would re-litigate a settled decision and risk drifting the frame toward the activation/trial language that's already been kept out (the 2026-08-07 snippets were rejected on exactly that ground).

2. The teammate-invite clarification belongs in the support line, as support-only copy — not as a tooltip, and not as a redesign of the affordance. The approved support-facing line is: *"Repo connection is the first recommended step. If another admin needs to join first, teammate invites can still be handled after that."* That sentence exists because Jake flagged the "blocked vs. deferred" confusion and Priya's ticket excerpt confirmed it ("We thought … meant the invite flow was blocked until the first repo finished connecting"). The clarification is a wording fix for an existing support pattern, not new surface area.

3. A new teammate-invite tooltip is out of scope. Comment C-241 on Frame 06 is still open on exactly that question — Priya asked whether teammate invite is in scope for launch-day activation, Marcus replied that if it stays, engineering needs empty, no-admin, and invite-failed states. A tooltip without those states is half a feature; a tooltip plus those states is a design pass. Neither belongs on a copy-clarification PR. This also matches the standing rule that tooltip/empty-state polish stays deferred unless it clearly changes activation evidence.

So: ship the support-line clarification as a copy-only change. Comment on the PR asking the author to drop the headline edit and the new tooltip from this PR, and reopen C-241 separately if Priya wants to actually scope teammate invite for launch (with the engineering states Marcus called out).

**Reconsider when:**

- Repo-first completion rate or teammate-invite confusion clearly regresses from the current baseline → reopen monitoring, and the support-line copy itself is in scope to revisit.
- Support volume on "blocked vs. deferred teammate invite" ticks up after the clarification lands → that would mean the support-line sentence didn't land and a tooltip (with the Marcus-flagged empty/no-admin/invite-failed states) is back on the table.
- Priya wants to formally answer C-241 (in-scope for launch-day activation vs. explicitly post-activation) and the answer is "in scope" → then the tooltip is a real design pass, not a one-line copy add, and it shouldn't ride along on a copy PR.

I can post that as the review comment on the PR if you want — want me to go ahead?

messages.content:
Three buckets is probably the cleanest way to walk in.

Bucket 1: things we explicitly can't do at 12 — coverage, parallel workstreams, whatever blocks Q3 in a way the team can't absorb or workaround.

Bucket 2: things we could do at 12 but only by trading something off. Usually a founder's attention or an existing person's roadmap. These are the "stretch" slots and they deserve the most honesty.

Bucket 3: things that'd be nice at 14 but don't actually gate Q3. Wants, not needs.

Devon's going to push on whether anything in bucket 1 truly can't be deferred — or whether it's bucket 3 wearing a bucket 1 hat. The litmus test: if Q3 was a coin flip, would we still make this hire? If yes → bucket 1, hire now. If no → bucket 3, defer to post-close.

Two things to be ready on regardless of which way Devon leans:

1. Specificity of "candidates on market." The strongest version is two specific people in motion and the window is real. The weakest is two reqs against a hypothetical pool. Devon will sniff out which one it is. If it's the strong version, name them. If it's the weak version, one req now + one held might be the honest call.

2. Success signal 90 days in. Your bear case is "explaining burn in every raise convo." The mitigation isn't "don't hire" — it's that by the time you're in the raise, the new hires have shipped something legible. Customer-visible feature, on-call rotation absorbed, whatever. That success metric should be in the req, not improvised. If you can't name it, the hire isn't ready.

On the onboarding risk: 2 same-week into 12 is the failure pattern. Cheap fixes are stagger (2-3 weeks apart), pre-written onboarding doc before day 1, one owner who isn't in flux themselves — Priya is the obvious one given her onboarding flow work just landed. None of those cost a hire; they're the cost of opening the req at all.

tests.request: Create an archive note explaining whether Evergreen's January 2024 current-flow examples pack was cleared to circulate and whether it constituted a complete procurement/security packet.

input.body:
Archive note — 2026-09-14

Subject: Evergreen's January 2024 current-flow examples pack — clearance to circulate, and whether it constituted a complete procurement/security packet.

1. What the pack was
- On January 5, 2024 at 9:27 AM PST, Sarah Kim emailed a final Evergreen pack to Morgan Chen, Devon Hayes, Jake, and Leo Park, subject "Re: Evergreen example cases to turn into current-flow pack".
- The pack was the circulate-now, current-flow examples pack (the v0.9 set): concrete examples of the bounded Mercury flow — first admin path, second admin path, delayed first live sync, invite/resend, source connect/disconnect, audit-history answer, and a materials/routing clarification. It described Scaffold as it works today. Internal guardrails were "current" wording only, no dates, no roadmap framing.

2. Clearance to circulate
- Cleared to circulate internally. Reviewers told Sarah the example format was usable for internal routing, which is why she sent the final pack on January 5.
- The pack, plus the bounded-flow summary and written current-state answers already on the thread, were explicitly designated the present-state materials to circulate internally for review now.
- No additional current-state written materials existed to attach at that time. Anything new that surfaced in Evergreen's internal review was to come back through the existing thread.

3. Was it a complete procurement/security packet?
- No. It was not a complete procurement/security packet, and it was never framed as one.
- The pack was deliberately bounded to present-state, current-flow examples only. Commercial/procurement framing was kept out of it on purpose.
- Items outside the pack — SSO/SAML, admin-side audit history, admin-vs-billing-owner separation, and the broader procurement/security packaging — belonged to a separate commercial/procurement lane on the Scaffold side, with Devon Hayes as the owner of that lane. No Evergreen-specific commitment, timing, or packet promise was tied to them.
- The fuller standalone procurement/security packet was treated as separate packaging work still being put together, to be shared on the thread only when there was something concrete. Sarah's December 11, 2023 forward of a first standalone procurement/security packet was the start of that separate workstream, not a completion of it; the January 5 pack did not subsume or replace it.

4. Status going in
- Cleared to circulate internally as present-state material, on the existing Evergreen customer thread, with Devon cc'd as the commercial/procurement contact.
- Not cleared (and never claimed) as a complete procurement/security packet. The procurement/security lane stayed separate, with no dates and no Evergreen-only concessions.
